extracted.intended_audience: educated readers of moral/philosophical essays; people seeking practical/ethical guidance on living, illness, and aging
extracted.subtask_description: A personal-philosophical essay giving practical and moral guidance about speech, conduct, coping with disease, aging, diet, exercise, and child-rearing; blends observations, maxims, and examples. Extracts prescriptive principles embedded in Montaigne's prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust voice/tone to subject and audience
rubrics_metrics.description: “Speak according to the affair you are speaking about to your auditor,” — the tone and motion of the voice carry much of the expression and signification of meaning; one should govern one’s voice to make oneself understood; there is a voice to instruct, a voice to flatter, and a voice to reprehend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose tone deliberately: aim not merely that your voice reach the listener but that it 'strike and pierce' when needed. Examples/antipatterns: speaking loudly for its own sake; dismissive valet reply (mocking the idea of merely being audible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Listeners must prepare themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: “Speaking is half his who speaks, and half his who hears; the latter ought to prepare himself to receive it,” — the hearer shares responsibility by adjusting readiness according to the speaker’s manner and the nature of the message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: tennis—receiver adjusts according to the striker. Implies mutual responsibility for effective communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ruinous impatience in the face of evils
rubrics_metrics.description: “We ruin ourselves by impatience. Evils have their life and limits, their diseases and their recovery.” — do not attempt to cut natural processes imperiously; impatience lengthens and multiplies ailments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule: grant diseases their course when appropriate; aggressive attempts to force outcomes can worsen matters. Philosophical balance between stubborn opposition and cowardly surrender is recommended (Crantor’s opinion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit Nature to take its own way
rubrics_metrics.description: “Let us a little permit Nature to take her own way; she better understands her own affairs than we.” — trust natural processes rather than over-intervening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: some maladies resolve without art; unnecessary medical meddling can prolong suffering. Moderation between action and resignation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept pleasant remedies and pleasures as profit
rubrics_metrics.description: “If it be a delicious medicine, take it: ‘tis always so much present good. Pleasure is one of the chiefest kinds of profit.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not disdain remedies (or comforts) for their name or colour if they are pleasant and effective — value immediate, agreeable relief as real benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endure unavoidable suffering; mix goods and evils
rubrics_metrics.description: “We must learn to suffer what we cannot evade; our life... is composed of contrary things... we should mingle the goods and evils which are consubstantial with our life.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy with music: a musician must use all tones. Moral: recognize necessity of both pleasure and pain; attempting to eliminate natural necessities is folly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage the imagination to lessen distress
rubrics_metrics.description: “I use my imagination as gently as I can, and would discharge it, if I could, of all trouble and contest; a man must assist, flatter, and deceive it, if he can.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques: reason with oneself, provide consolatory narratives (e.g., reframing disease as common, dignified, or instructive). If symptoms worsen, devise new stratagems to amuse or reassure the imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep records of symptoms and experience for consolation
rubrics_metrics.description: “For want of natural memory, I make one of paper; and as any new symptom happens in my disease, I set it down... turning over these little loose notes... I never fail of finding matter of consolation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical tip: record past favorable prognostics and experiences to counter present fear; experience and custom create hope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on actual sensation rather than speculative prognostics
rubrics_metrics.description: “I only judge of myself by actual sensation, not by reasoning... since I am resolved to bring nothing to it but expectation and patience?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid anxiety generated by doctors’ fearful prognostications and speculative interpretations; attend to bodily sensations and practice patient expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make fear its own disease
rubrics_metrics.description: “He who fears he shall suffer, already suffers what he fears.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid anticipatory suffering and anxiety; mental agitation can produce or lengthen real suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor activity and vigilance; life is movement
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is nothing that ought so much to be recommended to youth as activity and vigilance — our life is nothing but movement.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep physically active to maintain health and resist sloth; moderate sleeping and avoid habitual excess sleep when it produces heaviness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust exercise to bodily capacity as one ages
rubrics_metrics.description: “My body is capable of a firm, but not of a violent or sudden agitation... I escape of late from violent exercises... my limbs grow weary before they are warm.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer steady, moderate activity (walking, riding) over violent exercise in old age; tailor exertion to present capacities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embrace professions and company that cultivate courage
rubrics_metrics.description: Military life is praised as pleasant and noble; “company encourages even children” — exposure to shared danger builds courage and steadiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntariness in facing hazards ‘for the lustre and importance’ of action is ennobling; fortify oneself by practice and company rather than avoiding all risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice temperance and plainness in diet
rubrics_metrics.description: “Not to make good cheer with what another is enjoying, and to be curious in what a man eats, is the essence of this vice... Whoever cures a child of an obstinate liking for brown bread, bacon, or garlic, cures him also of pampering his palate.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simple, ordinary foods; avoid pampering the palate and excessive delicacy. Avoid over-nicety and luxury that cause tedium.

rubrics_metrics.name: When fasting or dieting, control exposure to temptation
rubrics_metrics.description: “When I design to fast I must be kept apart from the suppers, and must have only so much given me as is required for a prescribed collation; for if to table, I forget my resolution.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule to succeed in self-denial: remove access to the object of temptation; keep apart from abundant food when fasting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid long sittings at table and speaking on a full stomach
rubrics_metrics.description: “Long sittings at table both trouble me and do me harm... I tire and hurt myself with speaking upon a full stomach, as much as I find it very wholesome and pleasant to argue and to strain my voice before dinner.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep meals short; avoid engaging in strenuous conversation or activity immediately after heavy eating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use diet and natural processes as purgation rather than violent cures
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne argues the stone and some diseases can act as purgation; he values natural evacuations and warns that violent 'cures' (caustics, incisions, setons) can bring people to their graves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer less violent, more tolerable modes of dealing with bodily excesses; accept some natural purgations as beneficial rather than over-treating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer helping those in need over currying favor with the powerful
rubrics_metrics.description: “I am naturally more apt to follow the example... who rather gave his assistance to those who had most need of him than to those who had power to do him good.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral criterion for compassion and public conduct: assist the needy rather than seeking advantage from the powerful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instill frugality and hardship in child rearing by exposure to common conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: “Never take upon yourselves, and much less give up to your wives, the care of their nurture; leave the formation to fortune, under popular and natural laws; leave it to custom to train them up to frugality and hardship.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring up children among common people and rough conditions to habituate them to frugality rather than pampering them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meditate on death as consolation and natural end
rubrics_metrics.description: “I, in truth, receive a principal consolation in meditating my death, that it will be just and natural.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflection on mortality reduces fear; accepting death as natural supplies philosophical comfort in aging and illness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-consultation and the medico-magisterial fopperies
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctors can 'surfeit your ears with their prognostics' and produce agitation; their many false prognostics and expositions of nature's designs should caution us to distrust excessive prognostication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let repeated alarming prognoses unsettle your judgment; be wary of medical dogmatism that causes agitation without benefit.
